mainEntity.name: How much does a general contractor cost?

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a contractor and a general contractor?

mainEntity.name: Why does my Laurel finished basement need moisture-barrier carpet padding?

Moisture-barrier padding blocks that moisture transmission. mainEntity.name: How does DMV General Contracting Group protect trees during deck construction in Cabin John?

acceptedAnswer.text: Tree protection is a mandatory first step on every Cabin John deck project — not an afterthought. We map the Critical Root Zone (CRZ) of every significant tree near the proposed deck footprint before any post locations are proposed. We design extended beam spans to bridge root zones where possible, use hand tools within CRZs where excavation is unavoidable, plan equipment access routes to avoid driving over root zones, and document significant trees on permit drawings as required by the Montgomery County Forest Conservation Law.

mainEntity.name: What deck type works best for Cabin John's sloped lots?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on where your home's rear door sits relative to the grade. For walkout basement homes — where an existing door opens at basement level to the downhill rear yard — a walkout-level deck is the most natural and cost-effective option. For homes where the main living floor is significantly elevated above the rear grade, an elevated rear deck with variable-height posts following the slope is the most functional configuration. Multi-level decks that step between both levels are the most complete solution for homes with both configurations. DMV General Contracting Group assesses your specific terrain configuration during the free consultation.

mainEntity.name: Is Ipe hardwood a good choice for Cabin John decks?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — particularly for homeowners who want a material that ages into the Cabin John landscape rather than maintaining an artificially maintained suburban look. Ipe's warm brown weathers to a distinguished silver-grey over 12–18 months if left unfinished — a color that integrates beautifully with Cabin John's grey-brown bark and stone. Its 40–75 year lifespan, Class A fire resistance, and genuine natural wood character make it well-suited to this setting. Pre-drilling every fastener location and sealing every cut end are essential correct Ipe installation practices — DMV General Contracting Group's carpenters are trained in both.

The correct default specification for Cabin John homes is LVP (fully waterproof, dimensionally stable) until crawlspace encapsulation is completed and moisture levels are confirmed to be within hardwood installation tolerances. Solid hardwood is the highest-risk specification in Cabin John and should only be considered where moisture has been conclusively addressed.

mainEntity.name: What is heart pine and why is it important for DC rowhouse floors?

acceptedAnswer.text: Heart pine — longleaf pine — was the dominant flooring material in DC rowhouses built between approximately 1880 and 1930. DC rowhouse heart pine floors that have survived under carpet for 50–80 years are made from a material that is no longer commercially available. When these floors are viable for refinishing — which is often, given how long they were protected under carpet — restoring them preserves genuinely irreplaceable material at $3–$6 per square foot. mainEntity.name: How do you know if a wall is load-bearing in a Bethesda colonial?

acceptedAnswer.text: Load-bearing walls in Bethesda's colonials run perpendicular to the floor joists, are positioned over or adjacent to the foundation, and carry the weight of the floor or roof above. mainEntity.name: What is temporary shoring and why is it needed for load-bearing wall removal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Temporary shoring is a system of posts and beams installed on both sides of a load-bearing wall before any part of the wall is cut or removed. It transfers the structural load from the wall to the floor temporarily while the permanent beam is installed. Without temporary shoring, removing a load-bearing wall — even partially — can cause the structure above to shift or settle. DMV General Contracting Group installs temporary shoring as a standard step before every load-bearing wall removal, regardless of span or scope.

Combined with dense mature tree canopy that reduces sunlight and slows surface drying after rain, North Bethesda's hardscape surfaces stay wet significantly longer than comparable surfaces in open suburban MoCo communities. acceptedAnswer.text: Thermal-finish bluestone is the top choice for North Bethesda patios — the micro-textured thermal surface provides slip resistance even when damp or carrying algae film, and the thermal process slightly seals the stone's pores, slowing moisture absorption and algae colonization. Tumbled flagstone is the naturalistic alternative. Smooth sawn bluestone and polished or honed porcelain surfaces are not recommended — they become dangerously slippery in North Bethesda's wet conditions.

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — drainage design is the single most important element of any North Bethesda hardscape project. DMV General Contracting Group designs every North Bethesda hardscape drainage-first — slope, French drains, and channel drains planned before any surface material is selected.

mainEntity.name: How long does a concrete driveway last in Bethesda, MD?

acceptedAnswer.text: A properly installed concrete driveway in Bethesda lasts 30–50 years with basic maintenance — far longer than asphalt (15–20 years) and comparable to pavers. Key longevity factors are proper base preparation, minimum 4,000 PSI air-entrained concrete, steel reinforcement, correct control joint spacing, and sealing every 3–5 years. Avoid chloride-based ice melts on new concrete for the first winter — they accelerate surface scaling.

mainEntity.name: What is stamped concrete and is it a good choice for Bethesda patios?

acceptedAnswer.text: Stamped concrete uses rubber stamps to imprint patterns (slate, cobblestone, brick, wood plank) into freshly poured concrete, combined with integral color for a realistic natural material appearance. It is an excellent choice for Bethesda patios — offering the look of natural stone or pavers at 30–50% less cost, with a seamless surface (no joints for weeds) and durability in Maryland's climate. It requires resealing every 2–3 years to maintain color and sheen. DMV General Contracting Group installs stamped concrete patios throughout Bethesda.

mainEntity.name: Concrete vs. pavers — which is better for a Bethesda driveway or patio?

Pavers offer easier individual repair, better drainage, and a more premium appearance that Bethesda buyers tend to prefer at the high end of the market. Stamped concrete bridges the gap — delivering a paver-like appearance at closer to concrete pricing. DMV General Contracting Group installs both and provides an honest recommendation based on your goals and budget during the free consultation.

mainEntity.name: How long does concrete take to cure in Bethesda?

acceptedAnswer.text: Concrete reaches approximately 70% strength in 7 days and full design strength at 28 days. Foot traffic is safe after 24–48 hours. Vehicle traffic should wait 7 days minimum. mainEntity.name: How do I verify a contractor’s MHIC license in Maryland?

acceptedAnswer.text: Visit the Maryland Department of Labor's licensing portal at labor.maryland.gov/pq and search by contractor name or license number. You can also call MHIC at 410-230-6231. The lookup shows current status, expiration, and any disciplinary history.

mainEntity.name: What is the MHIC Guaranty Fund, and how does it protect me?

acceptedAnswer.text: The Maryland Home Improvement Guaranty Fund compensates homeowners for monetary losses caused by a licensed contractor's failure to perform or poor workmanship up to $30,000 per homeowner. It only applies when the contractor is licensed. Unlicensed operators give you no coverage at all.

mainEntity.name: How many quotes should I get for a Maryland home renovation?

acceptedAnswer.text: Three is the minimum, not the goal. For larger jobs, five quotes are reasonable. What matters more than the number is that every contractor bids on the same scope.

mainEntity.name: Can a Maryland contractor start work without a signed contract?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Maryland’s Home Improvement Law requires a written, signed contract before any work begins or money is paid. Any contractor who resists this requirement is already revealing something important.

mainEntity.name: What should the deposit be for a home renovation in Maryland?

acceptedAnswer.text: Maryland law caps the initial deposit at one-third of the total contract price. Plenty of reputable contractors will accept 10 to 15% at signing. Final payment should always wait until the walkthrough is done and you are satisfied.

mainEntity.name: Do I need permits for a kitchen or bathroom remodel in Maryland?

acceptedAnswer.text: Almost always yes, particularly when plumbing, electrical, or structural work is involved. Your contractor should pull all required permits. Unpermitted work can stop a home sale in its tracks and void your homeowner’s insurance.
